title: Dark Venture: Battle of the Ancients - a look at the pre-production game and expansions
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LRySNa5Y0No

Near-final production copies arrive and Daniel (@dungeondive) opens all three boxes — Battle of the Ancients plus the Beasts and Eggman and Kings and Heroes expansions — largely to discover what is in them alongside everyone watching.

The five base factions get laid out: Orbital gate masters, egg-hatching Dargon, gelatinous Bonework, self-mutating Vorpin, and the Alder King, a murdered ruler whose collector will stop at nothing to drag him back into the world. The map is double-sided, overland on one face and underground on the other, and Robert Lemon's building overlays stack upward — a tower or a ruined laboratory gains a second floor as you climb it.

Three ways to play: scenario, adventure and victory game. The adventure mode is the one Daniel expects to live in — an open-world narrative played cooperatively, where event tokens on the map unlock passages from a storybook, much as Dark Venture's location guides do. Thirteen scenarios fill book A, nearly all of them solo-capable, and a faction guide is printed on the flip side of book B, which he singles out as the thing most tactical games omit.

Also here: per-faction auto-enemy AI decks, secret reward cards that quietly seed new items in as you finish scenarios, Darvin the Sour selling potions and contracts, and a Kingsguard with an armoury deck of its own. Two announcements land in passing — a Dark Venture reprint, and his solo rules going official.

----

Overlay tiles that build into upper floors, or a faction guide bound into the scenario book — which small production decision has done the most for a game you own?
